641.quote_or_event: “Those who having investigated the Law expound it, are awakened and put an end to mundane existence; able to liberate both (themselves and others), they answer the well-deliberated questions.”
641.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on the ideal monk counts the ability to expound the Law clearly as a gift of its own, one that frees both the speaker and those who hear him.
641.tie_back: Valluvar calls goodness of the tongue a wealth in its own right; the Jain verse likewise gives skilled exposition a distinct worth, since it benefits others as well as oneself.
641.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
641._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Only a partial fit: the verse praises expounding the Law, but it does not rank eloquence as a possession separate from all other goods, which is the kural's actual claim.

642.quote_or_event: “A monk or a nun, well considering, should not use speech whether truth or untruth, or truth mixed with untruth, if it be sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, coarse, hard, leading to sins, to discord and factions, to grief and outrage, to destruction of living beings.”
642.explanation: In the Acaranga's lecture on modes of speech, every word is weighed before it is spoken, because speech can lead to sin, discord, grief and even the destruction of life.
642.tie_back: The kural warns that both gain and ruin come through speech, so one must guard against any slip; the Jain rule turns that same care into a discipline of considering each word first.
642.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
642._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong on the harm speech can do and the need for care; the Jain text says little about the good that speech brings, which is the other half of the kural.

643.quote_or_event: “The gods, men, Sabaras, and animals took the language of the Lord for their own.”
643.explanation: Jain tradition holds that when Mahavira preached, every listener, human or animal, understood him as if he spoke in their own tongue. Jacobi records this from the commentator Devendra in a note on the Uttaradhyayana.
643.tie_back: The kural defines true eloquence as speech that binds those who hear it and draws even those who have not heard it; the Jain image of the Jina's sermon captivating every kind of being is an idealised form of that power.
643.source: Verse quoted by Devendra's commentary, in Hermann Jacobi's footnote to Uttarādhyayana Sūtra, Lecture 2 (SBE 45, 1895, footnote on p. 8; sacred-texts.com)
643._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com ('*S*abaras' simplified to 'Sabaras'). This comes from a later commentator quoted in Jacobi's footnote, not from the canonical verse itself, and it concerns the Jina's supernatural speech rather than a human skill.

644.quote_or_event: “He who follows (the instruction) may believe something untrue; (one should) kindly (tell him) 'It is thus or thus.' One should never hurt him by outrageous language, nor give long-winded explanations of difficult passages. (If the pupil does not understand his short explanation), he should explain at greater length. When the pupil has heard it, he will correctly understand the Truth.”
644.explanation: The monk who teaches is told to fit his explanation to the hearer: kindly and briefly at first, then at greater length if the pupil has not understood.
644.tie_back: Valluvar says to speak only after knowing the nature of one's hearers; the Sutrakritanga gives a concrete method for shaping speech to what the listener can take in.
644.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
644._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good fit on adapting speech to the hearer; the kural's further claim that no virtue or wealth exceeds such speech has no counterpart here.

645.quote_or_event: “Well considering (what one is to say), speaking with precision, one should employ language in moderation and restraint.”
645.explanation: The Acaranga asks the monk to weigh every word, down to number, gender and tense, before speaking, so that what he says is exact and cannot be faulted.
645.tie_back: The kural says to speak only after making sure no other word can defeat one's own; the Jain rule of careful, precise speech aims at the same unassailable word.
645.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
645._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shares the stress on deliberate, precise wording, but the Jain aim is truthfulness and avoiding sin rather than winning a debate in council.

646.quote_or_event: “Will those who are not born of a good family, no matter how much learning they have acquired, will they become sufficiently wise to pass over, without censuring, the faults which occur in the speech of others?”
646.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on conduct in assemblies treats overlooking the faults in other people's speech as a mark of the truly cultivated.
646.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads the kural's 'taking the fruit of others' words' as grasping their substance while passing over faults in their wording; the Naladiyar names exactly that generous listening.
646.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 10 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
646._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. A Tamil Jain didactic text, not canonical scripture. It matches the listening half of the kural, but not the first half on speaking so that others long to hear.

647.quote_or_event: “A monk living single should not ridicule heretical doctrines, and should avoid hard words though they be true; he should not be vain, nor brag, but he should without embarrassment and passion (preach the Law). A monk should be modest though he be of a fearless mind.”
647.explanation: The ideal Jain preacher speaks without embarrassment and with a fearless mind, yet without hard words, boasting or passion.
647.tie_back: The kural describes the speaker who is strong, does not slip and does not fear; the Jain preacher shares the fearlessness and composure, though his goal is to teach, not to defeat rivals.
647.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.21–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
647._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote markers removed). Good on fearless, unflustered speech, but Jainism frowns on the contest and victory over opponents (ikal vellal) that the kural takes for granted.

648.quote_or_event: “But in that case they should say: 'N. N.! O long-lived one! O long-lived ones! O layman! O pupil! O faithful one! O lover of faith!' Considering well, they should use such sinless, blameless, &c., speech.”
648.explanation: Instead of abusive words, the monk is told to address people with courteous, kindly forms of speech that cause no offence.
648.tie_back: The kural says the world quickly does the bidding of those who speak in good order and pleasantly; the Jain rule supplies the pleasant, courteous manner, though not the promise of ready obedience.
648.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
648._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Next-best match only: it covers pleasant speech but has nothing on orderly arrangement or on speech winning the world's swift compliance.

649.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
649.explanation: The opening lecture on discipline warns the pupil against talkativeness and links it to the worthless, as opposed to valuable knowledge.
649.tie_back: Valluvar says those who love to say many words are those unable to say a few faultless ones; the Jain verse likewise sets idle talk against what has real worth.
649.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
649._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shares the warning against wordiness, but it does not make the kural's diagnosis that wordiness comes from lacking the skill to speak briefly.

650.quote_or_event: “Those learned men who collect plenty of books bring them and fill up every room in their houses, and yet understand them not, are of one kind, while those learned men who both understand their purport and are able to explain them to others are of another kind.”
650.explanation: The Naladiyar separates the learned who merely hoard books from those who understand them and can explain them to others.
650.tie_back: The kural likens those who cannot explain what they have learned to flowers without scent; the Naladiyar draws the same line between learning that stays shut away and learning that can be passed on.
650.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
650._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Close match on the need to communicate learning, without the kural's flower simile. It is a Tamil Jain text close to the Kural's own milieu, not canonical scripture.
